blocks.preview: Formatting

blocks.html: There are two ways to change the formatting options: flags, and manipulators. You can think of flags as boolean variables that can be turned on and off. Manipulators are objects placed in a stream that affect the way things are input and output.

blocks.html: There’s one other bit of trickiness when using setf() that needs to be mentioned. Many flags belong to groups, called format groups. A format group is a group of flags that perform similar (sometimes mutually exclusive) formatting options. For example, a format group named “basefield” contains the flags “oct”, “dec”, and “hex”, which controls the base of integral values. By default, the “dec” flag is set. Consequently, if we do this:
blocks.preview: There’s one other bit of trickiness when using setf() that needs to be mentioned

blocks.code:
std::cout.setf(std::ios::hex); // try to turn on hex output
std::cout << 27 << '\n';
blocks.html:
std::cout.setf(std::ios::hex); // try to turn on hex output
std::cout << 27 << '\n';
We get the following output:
blocks.preview: We get the following output:

blocks.html: 27

It didn’t work! The reason why is because setf() only turns flags on -- it isn’t smart enough to turn mutually exclusive flags off. Consequently, when we turned std::hex on, std::ios::dec was still on, and std::ios::dec apparently takes precedence. There are two ways to get around this problem.

blocks.html: First, we can turn off std::ios::dec so that only std::hex is set:
blocks.preview: First, we can turn off std::ios::dec so that only std::hex is set:

blocks.html:
std::cout.unsetf(std::ios::dec); // turn off decimal output
std::cout.setf(std::ios::hex); // turn on hexadecimal output
std::cout << 27 << '\n';
Now we get output as expected:
blocks.preview: Now we get output as expected:

blocks.html: 1b

The second way is to use a different form of setf() that takes two parameters: the first parameter is the flag to set, and the second is the formatting group it belongs to. When using this form of setf(), all of the flags belonging to the group are turned off, and only the flag passed in is turned on. For example:

std::cout.setf(std::ios::hex, std::ios::basefield);
std::cout << 27 << '\n';

In general, using manipulators is much easier than setting and unsetting flags. Many options are available via both flags and manipulators (such as changing the base), however, other options are only available via flags or via manipulators, so it’s important to know how to use both.

blocks.html: Width, fill characters, and justification
blocks.preview: Width, fill characters, and justification

blocks.html: Typically when you print numbers, the numbers are printed without any regard to the space around them. However, it is possible to left or right justify the printing of numbers. In order to do this, we have to first define a field width, which defines the number of output spaces a value will have. If the actual number printed is smaller than the field width, it will be left or right justified (as specified). If the actual number is larger than the field width, it will not be truncated -- it will overflow the field.
